Border War.
Vo. July 22.
LYNCHBURG, Va., July 23.—A party of men from McDowell County, W. Va., rode into Pocahontas and began firing their guns promiscuously in the streets. The town sergeant summoned a posse and attempted to arrest them when the invaders opened fire on them, wounding several of the sergeant's force. After quite a battle the officers succeeded in arresting two of the mob and lodged them in jail. The rest of them escaped by riding over the state line. Later in the evening the rumor was current that an attempt would be made to rescue the prisoners and the mayor ordered out the military.
charles-smith-pocahontas-1890-08-03.A4:
A Bloody Fight.
CHARLESTON, W. VA., July 24. — Particulars have just reached here of a bloody fight and riot in Pocahontas Va., Sunday night. Early in the afternoon a body of about twenty desperadoes headed by the notorious Jim Skinner, the well-known moonshiner, rode into town and began drinking whiskey. In a few hours they became riotous, flourishing their revolvers and firing at negroes as they passed. After two colored had been seriously wounded the citizens and the town authorities arrived to suppress the band and a general fight ensued. Two of the mob were shot and captured, while Charles Smith an unknown negro resident of Pocahontas received serious wounds, being shot in the head and arms.

The desperadoes fled back to West Virginia, where they have their headquarters in the mountains. A rumor reached Pocahontas Monday night that they would return to rescue their comrades, and it created such alarm that the mayor ordered out a posse of sixty men, who are now patrolling the town in expectation of an attack.

A DEMOCRAT CONGRESSMAN OUSTED

WASHINGTON, D. C., Aug. 5. — It took just ten minutes this morning for the house committee on elections to adopt the report declaring Representative Breckenridge not elected from the second district of Arkansas. A full attendance of republican members was obtained this morning and the report adopted with but a single dissenting vote against it, that of Marsh, the only democrat present.

The above is taken from the "Kansas Newspaper Union." Nothing can be more certain then the fact that the Election Bill, now before Congress, is the remedy needed for the ills of the South. This Dispatch above quoted, is self-contradictory—in one breath we are told that the Blacks refrained from voting—and in the next we are led to understand that they tried to take away the Ballot Box, the former assertion we believe to be true, and if he refrained from voting, it was simply because his life was in danger there as elsewhere in the South. By all means give us the Federal Election Bill, and in a few years we will have peace and quiet in that land of corn and cotton-a nation that cannot protect the humbliest of her citizens in the exercise of all civil and political rights is a failure.
